previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted with fever and right mandibular pain four days after a tooth extraction. She developed a fever post-dialysis and was found to have inflammatory changes in the right buccal and masticator spaces on CT, consistent with a soft tissue infection without abscess. She was initially treated with vancomycin, then transitioned to Unasyn and later discharged on oral Augmentin. Her fever resolved, and pain improved. During admission, she was noted to have mild transaminitis, likely due to simvastatin, which was held. She underwent scheduled hemodialysis, remained stable, and was discharged home in good condition with instructions to complete antibiotics, avoid alcohol and Tylenol, and follow up on liver tests.

Brief Hospital Course:
# RUQ pain and fever: A CT study done in the Emergency 
Department discovered a new hypodense lesion in the upper pole 
of the right kidney with perinephric stranding concerning for a 
nidus of infection, but there was no suspicion for any 
intra-abdominal processes.  While this finding was a likely 
source for her infection,  liver function tests revealed an 
elevated alkaline phosphatase and total bilirubin, which was 
concerning for a cholestatic process, such as a retained common 
bile duct stone, which would be consistent with her colicky pain 
that she described.  She was seen by the transplant surgery team 
and they ruled out a small bowel obstruction.  Abdominal 
ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities in the biliary 
system, other than mild dilatation of intra and extrahepatic 
bile ducts.  Her liver function tests remained stable.  A renal 
ultrasound was done to better characterize the lesion on the 
right kidney.  It was not shown to have any cystic properties 
that would make it amenable to sampling and culture.  A TTE was 
done to rule out the possibility of septic emboli to the kidney 
and it showed symmetric left ventricular hypertrophy and 
pulmonary artery systolic hypertension, EF>60%, but no 
vegetations.  We felt that antibiotic coverage for a suspected 
perirenal abscess would be the most prudent and she was started 
on pip/tazo and vancomycin.  (She reported a Red Man syndrome in 
response to vancomycin, so we infused it slowly.)  While she 
continued to have mild abdominal pain well-controlled by her 
home doses of hydromorphone throughout her hospitalization, she 
did not show any signs of a worsening infection and was sent 
home on Cipro PO + Vancomycin IV to be dosed at her HD sessions 
for total of a 2-week course.  Because this regimen does not 
cover all possible organisms (i.e. enterococcus), she was 
instructed to take her temperature often and report back if 
febrile.
.
#Shortness of breath:  The patient received a CTA chest in the 
Emergency Department to rule out a pulmonary embolism.  Chest 
x-ray showed pleural effusions/interstitial infiltrates seen on 
CXR.  Fluid overload is a likely possibility for her shortness 
of breath, as it improved after dialysis.  It is a possibility 
that her RUQ pain could have caused some of her shortness of 
breath as well.  Her respiratory status was stable throughout 
her hospitalization and she was discharged without oxygen 
supplementation.  
.
# ESRD, secondary to lupus nephritis: Patient received HD on her 
normal ___, and ___ schedule while in house. Her 
electrolytes abnormalities were corrected and her breathing 
seemed to improve after dialysis.  The Renal team was consulted 
and have arranged for her to receive her vancomycin after her 
outpatient HD sessions for the 12 days. 
.

Discharge Instructions:
It was a pleasure treating you at ___ 
___.  You were admitted with abdominal pain, fevers, and 
shortness of breath.  A CT scan confirmed that you did not have 
a blood clot in your lungs, but a new finding was discovered on 
your right kidney. To better characterize this, we performed an 
ultrasound of your abdomen and decided to treat this bump on 
your kidney as an infection.  You were prescribed IV antibiotics 
and we controlled your abdominal pain with medications.  You 
felt much better and we will be discharging you on 12 days on 
antibiotics to complete a 14-day course.

Also, your liver tests were mildly elevated upon admission and 
the ultrasound helped us to rule out any obstructions near the 
site of your gallbladder system.  Transplant surgery was 
consulted on your case and did not believe that your issue was 
surgical.  Your tests improved over the next 2 days and we felt 
comfortable discharging you on the previously mentioned 
antibiotics.

When you go to hemodialysis on your regularly scheduled days, 
they will give you your Vancomycin dose.  You will be 
responsible for taking the Ciprofloxacin 500mg daily.  Before 
you finish your 2-week antibiotic course, we would like you to 
get a repeat ultrasound of your abdomen to monitor the response 
of this kidney finding to antibiotic therapy.

We would like you to take your temperature with a thermometer a 
few times a day.  If you develop a fever, we would highly 
recommend that you come back to the hospital for further 
antibiotic treatment.  There are a small group of bugs that are 
not covered by this regimen and you may need stronger IV 
antibiotics if your fevers return.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Fevers.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PA AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  The cardiac silhouette is minimally
enlarged.  Mediastinal and hilar contours are normal.  Bilateral pleural
effusions are small.  Note is made of mild peribronchial cuffing and
interstitial opacity.  Cholecystectomy clips are present in the upper abdomen.

IMPRESSION:  Cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and interstitial opacities,
findings which suggest hydrostatic edema from CHF or volume overload.  Note
that viral or other atypical infections may have a similar interstitial
pattern, and follow up radiographs after diuresis may be helpful in this
regard.

EXAM:  CT of the torso with contrast.

EXAM DATE:  ___.

CLINICAL INFORMATION:  ___ female with SOB, right lower quadrant pain
and history of failed renal transplant, recently removed.  

TECHNIQUE:  Chest CTA was performed without and with contrast with multiplanar
reformatted images provided. CT abd/pelvis was also performed utilizing a CTE
protocol with coronal and sagittal reformats. Oral contrast was administered.

FINDINGS:

CHEST:  Noncontrast imaging demonstrates no aortic intramural hematoma.
Following the administration of IV contrast, there is normal opacification of
the pulmonary arterial tree without filling defect to suggest the presence of
a pulmonary embolism. The thoracic aorta is normal in course and caliber
without evidence of dissection or aneurysm. The heart is mildly enlarged.
There is no pericardial effusion. There is calcification of the mitral valve
annulus and coronary arteries. 

Bilateral pleural effusions are present, right greater than left. There is no
lymphadenopathy though note is made of mediastinal edema with prominent
peribronchovascular fluid most compatible with pulmonary congestion.
Interlobular septal thickening and scattered ground glass opacity is likely
secondary to pulmonary edema. The possiblity of early infection cannot be
excluded. Left lower lobe scarring with subjacent atelectasis is noted. 

ABDOMEN:  The liver appears normal.  A splenic hypodensity is stable and may
represent a hemangioma.  The gallbladder is surgically absent. There is mild
intrahepatic biliary ductal prominence status post cholecystectomy.  The
pancreas appears normal.  The bilateral adrenals are unremarkable.  

The native kidneys enhance and appear atrophic. There is right perinephric
stranding with a focal hypodense lesion in the upper pole of the right kidney
measuring 1.6 x 1.8 x 2.2 cm. Findings are concerning for infection. 

The stomach is filled with contrast material, and is otherwise unremarkable. 
The duodenum is normal in appearance.  The proximal small bowel is distended
with contrast, but not dilated.  The distal small bowel is decompressed and no
distinct transition point is seen.  The small bowel mesentery is normal in
appearance. The aorta and its major branches appear patent, without aneurysmal
dilatation. There is moderate atherosclerotic change.  

PELVIS:  The rectum contains stool and air.  The colon is normal in
appearance.  The appendix is not seen.  Surgical clips are seen within the
right lower quadrant, adjacent to the right psoas likely reflecting recent
removal of renal transplant. There is hyperdensity along the right paracolic
gutter, likely represents post-surgical change. Patient is status post
hysterectomy. Urinary bladder is decompressed. 

Evaluation of the pelvic structures is limited by streak artifact from a right
total hip arthroplasty.

BONES:  A right total hip arthroplasty is seen, without obvious complications.
Sclerotic and mottled appearance of the bones likely secondary to renal
osteodystrophy. 

IMPRESSION:
1.  Findings compatible with fluid overload with pulmonary congestion, small
bilateral pleural effusions.  

2.  Right perinephric stranding with hypodense renal lesion in the upper pole
concerning for infection. 

These findings were discussed with Dr. ___ of transplant surgery at
9:45AM on ___.

HISTORY:  Lupus and end-stage renal disease status post failed renal
transplant that was removed.  Patient now with right upper quadrant abdominal
pain, fever and shortness of breath.

COMPARISON:  CT ___ and CT ___.

FINDINGS:  The liver is normal in echotexture.  No focal hepatic lesion is
identified.  The main portal vein is patent with hepatopetal flow.  There has
been a prior cholecystectomy.  The common bile duct is top normal in size
measuring approximately 6 mm, and does not appear to taper distally into the
pancreatic head, though this is without significant change compared to more
remote CTs dating back to ___.  No stone within the common bile duct
is identified.  There is also mild prominence of the intrahepatic bile ducts,
as seen on prior CTs.  

The right kidney measures 7.9 cm.  Within the upper pole is a 2.5 cm x 2.1 cm
x 2.2 cm rounded hypoechoic lesion without demonstrable color flow, which
likely reflects a focal area of bacterial nephritis.  No discrete drainable
collection is identified.  There is no perinephric collection.  Within the
lower pole of the right kidney is a 5-mm simple-appearing cyst.  The left
kidney measures 7.5 cm.  There is mild fullness of the left renal collecting
system, which is new compared to prior study.  Both kidneys are small and
diffusely echogenic, compatible with medical renal disease.  The spleen is
normal in size measuring 9.3 cm, with vascular calcifications noted.  The
pancreas is normal in appearance.  Partially visualized are small bilateral
pleural effusions.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Focal rounded hypoechoic lesion in the upper pole of the right kidney,
corresponding to the lesion identified on CT, ___.  This may reflect
a focal area of bacterial nephritis.  No discrete drainable collection or
perinephric collection is identified.
2.  Small echogenic kidneys bilaterally, compatible with medical renal
disease, with mild fullness of the left renal collecting system.
3.  Mild prominence of the intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts, similar in
appearance compared to more remote CTs dating back to ___.  No stones
within the common bile duct are identified.
